gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many watt-hours each bank actually puts into a laptop, or what that comes to per pound and per dollar. Macworld's MacBook Pro test scores work out to about 87.5 Wh for the Anker Prime 26K ($2.63 per delivered Wh, 66 Wh/lb) and about 64 Wh for the Anker 25K 165W ($1.86 per delivered Wh, 49 Wh/lb). Anker's own figure for the 25K 165W is 65 Wh, which agrees and means less than one full charge of a 70 Wh 14-inch MacBook Pro.
standout_why: I read Macworld (cited) in full. It gives rated mAh/Wh, weight, a 'best price today' and a Test Score: the percentages from two back-to-back recharges of a 14-inch M2 MacBook Pro, added together. It never turns that score into delivered Wh, Wh per lb or dollars per usable Wh, and it never gives the test laptop's battery size. The itechguides page (rank 1) says usable energy is lower than rated but gives no efficiency, charge count or cost per Wh. Wirecutter (cited) could not be opened because nytimes.com was blocked. thisusb.com and solargenadvisor.com failed with certificate errors. ChatGPT's answer itself only lists mAh and per-port watts.
decides: It argues against ChatGPT's Anker 25K 165W card. That bank turns its 90 Wh rating into about 64–65 Wh at the laptop, which is not a full charge of a 70 Wh 14-inch MacBook Pro. The Anker Prime 26K delivers about 87.5 Wh, a full charge plus about 25%. Per dollar, though, both Ankers are beaten by banks Macworld scored 119–120% at under $90 (INIU Cougar P64, EcoFlow RAPID Pro 27K). The UGREEN 145W keeps the best figures on rated specs ($0.89 per rated Wh, 81 rated Wh/lb), but no reviewer has measured what it delivers, so its value pick stays provisional until it is tested.
